source_refs.note: Practice short questions written from Chapter 2 (PDF 22-45, printed 22-45); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice short questions for the whole of Chapter 2 (Atomic Structure), arranged by the chapter's sections, in the style of a 2-mark Board short question. Each answer is a short model answer; small numericals show the working, and a comparison is answered as a table.
2.1 Atomic number, proton number and nucleon number; identity of an element

blocks.prompt: 1 What did Moseley observe in 1913, and what did he conclude about the atomic number?
blocks.explanation: When elements were bombarded with cathode rays, X-rays of characteristic frequencies were produced; √(frequency) ∝ Z. He concluded that the atomic number Z is a fundamental property of an element. It is also called proton number.

book_ref.quote: the square root of the frequency of the X-rays was directly proportional to the atomic number

blocks.prompt: 2 Define nucleon number and write its relation with atomic number and the number of neutrons.
blocks.explanation: The number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom together is its nucleon number (A), also called mass number. A = Z + N, so N = A − Z.

book_ref.quote: collectively called its nucleon number (A), also called mass number

blocks.prompt: 3 Calculate the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in ²³₁₁Na⁺.
blocks.explanation: Protons = Z = 11. Neutrons = A − Z = 23 − 11 = 12. Na loses one electron: electrons = 11 − 1 = 10.

book_ref.quote: the number of electrons, protons, and neutrons can be justified for an ion

blocks.prompt: 4 Show that ¹⁶₈O²⁻ and ¹⁹₉F⁻ have the same number of electrons but different numbers of neutrons.
blocks.explanation: O²⁻: electrons = 8 + 2 = 10; neutrons = 16 − 8 = 8. F⁻: electrons = 9 + 1 = 10; neutrons = 19 − 9 = 10. Both have 10 electrons; neutrons are 8 and 10.

book_ref.quote: In case electron gain happens by the neutral atoms

blocks.prompt: 5 An atom of ²⁴₁₂Mg forms Mg²⁺. Which of the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons change? Give the values.
blocks.explanation: Only electrons change. Protons = 12 and neutrons = 24 − 12 = 12 stay the same; electrons = 12 − 2 = 10.

book_ref.quote: atom loses three electrons to form Al³⁺

blocks.prompt: 6 Differentiate between atomic number and mass number.
blocks.explanation: Atomic number counts protons only; mass number counts protons and neutrons.

book_ref.quote: Thus the atomic number and proton number represent the same concept.

rows: Number of protons in the nucleus
Number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus
Same for every atom of an element; a fundamental property

blocks.text: 2.2 Effect of an electric field on the fundamental particles

blocks.prompt: 7 How do beams of electrons, protons and neutrons behave when passed at the same speed through an electric field?
blocks.explanation: Neutrons, being neutral, are not deflected and travel straight. Protons (positive) are deflected towards the negative plate. Electrons (negative) are deflected towards the positive plate, to a greater extent because they are 1/1836 times as heavy as protons.

book_ref.quote: If we allow the beams of electrons, protons and neutrons to pass one by one at the same speed

blocks.prompt: 8 Why are electrons deflected more than protons in an electric field?
blocks.explanation: Angle of deflection ∝ charge/mass. The electron and proton carry equal amounts of charge, but the electron's mass is only 1/1836 of the proton's, so its charge/mass is much larger and it is deflected more.

book_ref.quote: to greater extent since they are 1/1836 times lighter than protons

blocks.prompt: 9 Differentiate between the angle of deflection and the radius of deflection of a particle in an electric field.
blocks.explanation: Angle of deflection depends on charge/mass; radius of deflection on mass/charge.

book_ref.quote: the factors affecting the radius of deflection are reciprocal to that for the angle of deflection

rows: Measures deviation as an angle from the original direction
Measures deviation by imagining the particle moving in a circular path

blocks.prompt: 10 Calculate the charge-to-mass ratio (e/m) of a proton from the values in Table 2.2.

book_ref.quote: Table 2.2 Properties of three fundamental particles

blocks.prompt: 11 Using the masses in amu from Table 2.2, show that a proton is about 1836 times heavier than an electron.
blocks.explanation: Mass of proton/mass of electron = 1.0073 amu / 5.4858 × 10⁻⁴ amu = 1836. So the electron is 1/1836 of the proton's mass.

book_ref.quote: shows the properties of three fundamental particles electron, proton and neutron present in an atom

blocks.text: 2.3 Experimental evidence for the electronic configuration

blocks.prompt: 12 From which model does the modern theory of electronic structure originate, and what are the two main sources of evidence for it?
blocks.explanation: It originates from the Bohr model of the atom. Evidence for this and later models comes principally from (i) atomic spectra and (ii) ionization energies.

book_ref.quote: derives principally from two sources; atomic spectra and ionization energies

blocks.prompt: 13 What is an atomic emission spectrum?
blocks.explanation: When an element in its gaseous state is heated to high temperature or subjected to electrical discharge, it emits radiation of certain wavelengths. The spectrum of this radiation contains coloured lines and is called the atomic emission spectrum.

book_ref.quote: The spectrum of this radiation contains coloured lines and is called atomic emission spectrum.

blocks.prompt: 14 Differentiate between atomic emission spectrum and atomic absorption spectrum.
blocks.explanation: Emission gives coloured lines from a hot or excited gas; absorption gives dark lines from a cold gas in white light.

book_ref.quote: When a beam of white light is passed through a gaseous sample of an element in cold state, certain wavelengths are absorbed.

rows: Gaseous element is heated to high temperature or subjected to electrical discharge
White light is passed through the gaseous element in the cold state
Lines at the element's characteristic wavelengths
Dark lines at exactly the same wavelengths as the emission lines

blocks.prompt: 15 Why are atomic spectra called the finger prints of the elements?
blocks.explanation: Each element has a unique arrangement of electrons and so a unique set of fixed energy levels. The wavelengths emitted or absorbed when electrons jump between these levels are therefore unique, so every element has its own characteristic spectrum by which it is identified.

book_ref.quote: atomic spectra are the finger prints of the elements

blocks.prompt: 16 Why do the dark lines of the absorption spectrum of an element lie at the same wavelengths as the coloured lines of its emission spectrum?
blocks.explanation: Both arise from electrons jumping between the same fixed energy levels of that element. Energy absorbed for a jump up equals energy emitted for the same jump down, so the wavelengths are exactly the same.

book_ref.quote: the wavelengths and frequencies of the radiation absorbed or emitted when electrons jump from one energy level to another

blocks.text: 2.3.2 Relation between ionization energy and energy levels (electronic shells)

blocks.prompt: 17 What are successive ionization energies? Write the equations for the first three.
blocks.explanation:
The energies needed to remove the electrons of an atom one by one, until only the nucleus is left.
X → X⁺ + e⁻ (ΔHᵢ₁)
X⁺ → X²⁺ + e⁻ (ΔHᵢ₂)
X²⁺ → X³⁺ + e⁻ (ΔHᵢ₃)

book_ref.quote: We call this sequence of ionization energies, successive ionization energies.

blocks.prompt: 18 Why is the jump on removing the eleventh electron of magnesium even larger than the jump on removing its third electron?
blocks.explanation: The third electron is the first one taken from the second shell. The eleventh electron is the first one taken from the first, innermost shell, right next to the nucleus, where it is held far more strongly. So that jump is much more enormous.

book_ref.quote: A similar but much more enormous jump occurs when the eleventh and twelfth electrons are removed.

blocks.prompt: 19 Why are all ionization energies endothermic?
blocks.explanation: An electron is attracted by the nucleus, so energy must be supplied to separate it from the atom. Hence every ionization absorbs energy; ionization energies are strongly endothermic.

book_ref.quote: All ionization energies are strongly endothermic

blocks.prompt: 20 Arrange lithium, sodium and potassium in order of decreasing first ionization energy and give the reason.
blocks.explanation: Li > Na > K. Down the group the number of shells increases, the atom becomes larger and the hold of the nucleus on the valence electron decreases, so removal becomes easier.

book_ref.quote: down the group, number of shells increases, hold of nucleus on the valence electrons decreases

blocks.prompt: 21 Why does ionization energy generally increase across a period?
blocks.explanation: Across a period the shell number remains the same. The proton number increases while electrons are added to the same shell, so the nucleus attracts the valence electrons more strongly and ionization energy increases.

book_ref.quote: As the proton number increases, electrons are added in the same shell.

blocks.prompt: 22 The first four ionization energies of an element are 801, 2427, 3660 and 25026 kJ mol⁻¹. How many valence electrons does it have?
blocks.explanation: Increases: 2427 − 801 = 1626; 3660 − 2427 = 1233; 25026 − 3660 = 21366 kJ mol⁻¹ (ΔHᵢ₄/ΔHᵢ₃ = 6.8). The large jump comes after the third electron, so the fourth comes from an inner shell: the element has 3 valence electrons (group 13).

book_ref.quote: The successive ionization energies show clearly the arrangement of electrons in shells around the nucleus.

blocks.prompt: 23 Why does Schrödinger's model need three quantum numbers to describe orbitals, while the Bohr model used only one?
blocks.explanation: The Bohr model was one-dimensional; only the size and energy of the orbit mattered, given by n. Schrödinger's model lets the electron occupy three-dimensional space, which needs three coordinates, i.e. three quantum numbers n, ℓ and m (size, shape, orientation).

book_ref.quote: Since Schrodinger’s model allowed the electron to occupy three-dimensional space

blocks.prompt: 24 What does the principal quantum number describe? What is the effect of increasing n?
blocks.explanation: n (1, 2, 3, … = K, L, M, …) describes the size and energy of the orbital. The larger n is, the greater the average distance of the electron from the nucleus (larger orbital) and the higher its energy, so it is less tightly bound to the nucleus.

book_ref.quote: The larger ‘n’ is, the greater the average distance of an electron in the orbital from the nucleus

blocks.prompt: 25 Define an electron shell. Calculate the maximum number of electrons in the shells with n = 5 and n = 6.
blocks.explanation: An electron shell is the collection of orbitals with the same value of n. Maximum electrons = 2n²: for n = 5, 2 × 25 = 50; for n = 6, 2 × 36 = 72.

book_ref.quote: maximum number of electrons in a shell by the formula 2n²

blocks.prompt: 26 Define a subshell. Give the values of ℓ and the subshells for n = 4.
blocks.explanation: A subshell is the set of orbitals that have the same n and ℓ values. For n = 4, ℓ = 0, 1, 2, 3, giving the 4s, 4p, 4d and 4f subshells (four subshells, equal to the shell number).

book_ref.quote: The set of orbitals that have the same n and ℓ values is called a subshell.

blocks.prompt: 27 Why is there no 2d subshell?
blocks.explanation: ℓ can only take values from 0 to (n − 1). For n = 2, ℓ = 0 or 1 only (2s and 2p). A d subshell needs ℓ = 2, which is possible only when n is 3 or more.

book_ref.quote: can have integral values 0 to (n- 1) for each value of n

blocks.prompt: 28 Using the formula 2(2ℓ + 1), calculate the maximum number of electrons in the p and f subshells.
blocks.explanation: p subshell: ℓ = 1, 2(2 × 1 + 1) = 6 electrons. f subshell: ℓ = 3, 2(2 × 3 + 1) = 14 electrons.

book_ref.quote: The number of electrons in a subshell can be calculated by the formula 2(2ℓ+1)

blocks.prompt: 29 Differentiate between an electron shell and a subshell.
blocks.explanation: A shell is fixed by n alone; a subshell by n and ℓ together.

book_ref.quote: These are the spectral terms used to describe certain features of spectral lines.

rows: Collection of orbitals with the same value of n
Set of orbitals with the same n and ℓ values
Described by the principal quantum number n
Described by n together with the azimuthal quantum number ℓ
e.g. 2s and 2p of the L shell

blocks.prompt: 30 Write the values of the magnetic quantum number for ℓ = 3. How many orbitals does this subshell have?
blocks.explanation: m takes (2ℓ + 1) values from −ℓ to +ℓ: −3, −2, −1, 0, +1, +2, +3. These seven values mean the f subshell has 7 orbitals.

book_ref.quote: The magnetic quantum number ‘m’ describes the orientation of an orbital in space.

blocks.prompt: 31 What are degenerate orbitals? Why is m called the magnetic quantum number?
blocks.explanation: Orbitals of the same subshell have the same energy; they are degenerate orbitals (e.g. the three 2p orbitals). They are differentiated from each other only in the presence of a magnetic field, hence the name magnetic quantum number.

book_ref.quote: Orbitals of the same subshell have same energy and are called degenerate orbitals.

blocks.prompt: 32 Why does a d subshell have five orbitals?
blocks.explanation: For a d subshell ℓ = 2, and m has (2ℓ + 1) = 5 values: −2, −1, 0, +1, +2. The values of m give the number of orbitals, so the d subshell has 5 orbitals.

book_ref.quote: If ℓ=2, (d-subshell), there are five values of m

blocks.prompt: 33 Why does an electron behave like a magnet? What are the values of the spin quantum number?
blocks.explanation: An electron spins around its own axis, and a spinning charge generates a magnetic field, so it behaves like a magnet. The spin can be clockwise (s = +½, ↑) or anticlockwise (s = −½, ↓).

book_ref.quote: It is this motion that causes an electron to behave like a magnet.

blocks.prompt: 34 Why is a fourth quantum number needed when three quantum numbers already describe an orbital?
blocks.explanation: An orbital can hold two electrons, which have the same n, ℓ and m. The spin quantum number s (+½ or −½) is needed to differentiate between these two electrons.

book_ref.quote: Thus it takes three quantum numbers to describe an orbital

blocks.prompt: 35 Show that the shell with n = 3 has 3 subshells, 9 orbitals and at most 18 electrons.
blocks.explanation: Subshells = n = 3 (3s, 3p, 3d). Orbitals = 1 + 3 + 5 = 9 = n². Electrons = 2 per orbital = 2 × 9 = 18 = 2n².

book_ref.quote: there are n subshells consisting of n² orbitals with a maximum number of 2n² electrons

blocks.prompt: 36 Define an atomic orbital.
blocks.explanation: An atomic orbital is the three-dimensional region in space around the nucleus in which the probability of finding the electron is maximum.

book_ref.quote: the three dimensional region in space around the nucleus in which the probability of finding the electron is maximum

blocks.prompt: 37 Describe the shape of an s orbital. How does its size change with n?
blocks.explanation: An s orbital is spherical; the electron density around the nucleus is uniformly distributed in all directions. As the principal quantum number increases, the s orbital becomes larger (2s is larger than 1s).

book_ref.quote: With the increase in the principal quantum number, the size of s orbital also becomes larger.

blocks.prompt: 38 Differentiate between an s orbital and a p orbital.
blocks.explanation: An s orbital is spherical; a p orbital has two lobes on an axis.

book_ref.quote: The electron density is not distributed in a spherically symmetric fashion as in an s orbital.

rows: Electron density uniform in all directions
One s orbital in a subshell (m = 0)
Three p orbitals px, py, pz (m = −1, 0, +1)

blocks.prompt: 39 Describe the orientations of the five d orbitals.
blocks.explanation: dxy, dxz and dyz lie in the xy, xz and yz planes respectively. The lobes of dx²−y² lie along the x and y axes. dz² has two lobes along the z-axis and a doughnut in the xy plane.

book_ref.quote: In a given shell, ‘d’ orbitals have different shapes and orientations in space.

blocks.prompt: 40 How many f orbitals are there in an f subshell, and what does the chapter say about their shapes?
blocks.explanation: An f subshell (ℓ = 3) has seven orientations in space, so there are seven f orbitals (m = −3 to +3). Their shapes are very complicated.

book_ref.quote: An f subshell has seven orientations in space, i.e. there are seven f orbitals.

blocks.prompt: 41 Define electronic configuration. What does the notation 3p⁴ mean?
blocks.explanation: Electronic configuration is the distribution of electrons among the available shells, subshells or orbitals of an atom or ion. In 3p⁴, 3 is the shell, p the subshell and the superscript 4 the number of electrons in that subshell.

book_ref.quote: Each symbol has a superscript on the right.

blocks.prompt: 42 How are electrons shown in an orbital diagram? Write the subshell configuration of ¹⁹₉F.
blocks.explanation: Each group of orbitals is labelled by its subshell notation and each electron is shown by an arrow: up for s = +½, down for s = −½. F (9 electrons): 1s² 2s² 2p⁵.

book_ref.quote: An electron in an orbital is shown by an arrow.

blocks.prompt: 43 Give the maximum electron capacities of the K, L, M and N shells and the orbitals each contains.
blocks.explanation: K (n = 1): 2, in 1s. L (n = 2): 8, in 2s and 2p. M (n = 3): 18, in 3s, 3p and 3d. N (n = 4): 32, in 4s, 4p, 4d and 4f.

book_ref.quote: The shells, denoted as K, L, M, N, and so on, correspond to the principal quantum number (n) of the orbitals.

blocks.text: 2.7.2 Distribution of electrons in subshells and orbitals: the Aufbau principle

blocks.prompt: 44 State the Aufbau principle.
blocks.explanation: The Aufbau (building up) principle says that the subshells in an atom are filled with electrons in increasing order of their energy values; the order is found from the (n + ℓ) values.

book_ref.quote: the subshells in an atom are filled with electrons in an increasing order of their energy values

blocks.prompt: 45 State the (n + ℓ) rule. Which is filled first, 6s or 4f?
blocks.explanation: The subshell with the lower (n + ℓ) value has lower energy and is filled first; if (n + ℓ) is equal, the one with lower n is filled first. 6s: 6 + 0 = 6; 4f: 4 + 3 = 7. So 6s is filled before 4f.

book_ref.quote: The subshell having lower (n + ℓ) value has lower energy and is filled first.

blocks.prompt: 46 Calculate (n + ℓ) for 4d, 5p and 6s and arrange them in the order of filling.
blocks.explanation: 4d: 4 + 2 = 6; 5p: 5 + 1 = 6; 6s: 6 + 0 = 6. All equal, so lower n fills first: 4d < 5p < 6s.

book_ref.quote: then the subshell with lower

blocks.text: Pauli's exclusion principle (printed as a second 2.7.2)

blocks.prompt: 47 State Pauli's exclusion principle.
blocks.explanation: No two electrons in an atom can have the same values for all four quantum numbers; in other words, two electrons in an orbital always have opposite spins.

book_ref.quote: No two electrons in an atom can have the same values for all the four quantum numbers

blocks.prompt: 48 Write the four quantum numbers of the two electrons in the 3s orbital of magnesium.
blocks.explanation: Electron 1: n = 3, ℓ = 0, m = 0, s = +½. Electron 2: n = 3, ℓ = 0, m = 0, s = −½. They differ only in spin.

book_ref.quote: The two electrons having the same values of

blocks.prompt: 49 Why can an orbital not hold three electrons?
blocks.explanation: All electrons in one orbital have the same n, ℓ and m. The spin s has only two values, +½ and −½, so a third electron would repeat all four quantum numbers of one of the others, which Pauli's exclusion principle forbids.

book_ref.quote: Two electrons in an orbital will always have opposite spins

blocks.prompt: 50 State Hund's rule and use it to explain the number of unpaired electrons in a nitrogen atom (1s² 2s² 2p³).
blocks.explanation: When degenerate orbitals are available, electrons are placed in separate orbitals with the same spin rather than in the same orbital with opposite spins. So nitrogen's three 2p electrons go one each into 2px, 2py and 2pz with the same spin: 3 unpaired electrons.

book_ref.quote: they should be placed in separate orbitals with the same spin rather than in the same orbital with opposite spins

blocks.prompt: 51 Why do electrons occupy separate orbitals of the same subshell wherever possible?
blocks.explanation: Electrons in the same region of space repel each other because they have the same charge. Occupying separate orbitals (with the same spin) minimizes this repulsion; they pair only when no empty orbital is left in the subshell.

book_ref.quote: Electrons in the same region of space repel each other because they have the same charge.

blocks.prompt: 52 Write the configuration of manganese (Z = 25) from Table 2.7 and find the number of unpaired electrons in it.
blocks.explanation: Mn: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁵4s². The five 3d electrons occupy the five 3d orbitals singly with the same spin; all other subshells are full. Unpaired electrons = 5.

book_ref.quote: Electrons are only paired when there are no more empty orbitals available within a subshell.

blocks.prompt: 53 Identify the element with configuration 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d¹⁰4s²4p⁵ and state its atomic number.
blocks.explanation: Electrons = 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 + 10 + 2 + 5 = 35, so Z = 35: bromine (Br), as in Table 2.7.

book_ref.quote: Electronic configuration of ground states of elements

blocks.text: 2.8 Electronic configuration and the periodic table

blocks.prompt: 54 How is the outer configuration of an element related to its group? Give the outer configurations of groups 1, 2 and 13.
blocks.explanation: The periodic table places elements with the same pattern of outer-shell (valence) configuration in the same group. Group 1: ns¹; group 2: ns²; group 13: ns²np¹.

book_ref.quote: elements with the same pattern of outer-shell (valence) electron configuration are arranged in same groups

blocks.prompt: 55 Why does the d-block have ten columns and the f-block fourteen columns?
blocks.explanation: The number of columns in a block equals the number of electrons its subshell can hold. A d subshell holds 10 electrons and an f subshell 14, so the d-block has 10 columns and the f-block 14 (likewise s: 2, p: 6).

book_ref.quote: Recall that the numbers 2, 6, 10, and 14 are precisely the number of electrons that can fill the s, p, d, and f subshells

blocks.prompt: 56 Define valence electrons. Why do elements of the same group show similar chemical properties?
blocks.explanation: Valence electrons are the electrons in the outermost shell of an atom; they are primarily involved in chemical reactions. Elements of a group have similar valence-electron configurations, which account for their similar chemical properties.

book_ref.quote: These are such electrons that are primarily involved in chemical reactions.

blocks.text: 2.8.2 Classification of the elements of the periodic table

blocks.prompt: 57 Differentiate between representative elements and transition elements on the basis of electronic configuration.
blocks.explanation: Representative elements fill an outer s or p subshell; transition elements fill a d subshell.

book_ref.quote: Similarly, in the d-block transition elements, a ‘d’ subshell is being filled.

rows: A d subshell is being filled
Outer s or p subshell is being filled
s-block and p-block of the table
d-block, ten columns in the middle

blocks.prompt: 58 Which subshell is being filled in each of the four coloured areas of Figure 2.16?
blocks.explanation: Blue area: ns (s-block). Green area: np (p-block). Yellow area: (n − 1)d (d-block). Light golden area: (n − 2)f (f-block).

book_ref.quote: Figure 2.16 shows a periodic table indicating this pattern.

blocks.prompt: 59 Write the electronic configurations of Mg²⁺ (Z = 12) and O²⁻ (Z = 8). Which noble gas do they resemble?
blocks.explanation: Mg²⁺: 12 − 2 = 10 electrons, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶. O²⁻: 8 + 2 = 10 electrons, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶. Both have the configuration of neon.

book_ref.quote: Negative ions are formed when atoms gain electrons.

blocks.prompt: 60 Mn is 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁵4s². Write the configuration of Mn²⁺ and give the reason.
blocks.explanation: Mn²⁺: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁵. Although 4s fills before 3d, a d-block atom loses its 4s electrons first when it forms an ion.

book_ref.quote: But when atoms of a d-block element lose electrons to form ions, the 4s electrons are lost first.

blocks.prompt: 61 Differentiate between the formation of positive and negative ions with one example each.
blocks.explanation: A positive ion forms by losing electrons; a negative ion by gaining them.

book_ref.quote: Positive ions are formed when electrons are removed from atoms.

rows: Formed when electrons are removed from an atom
Formed when an atom gains electrons

blocks.prompt: 62 Define a free radical and give three examples.
blocks.explanation: A free radical is a species that has one or more unpaired electrons, shown by a dot. Examples: chlorine atom Cl•, and the groups OH• and CH₃•.

book_ref.quote: Apart from single atoms, groups of atoms can also be free radicals.

blocks.prompt: 63 Why is a free chlorine atom a free radical? In which subshell is its unpaired electron?
blocks.explanation: Cl: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵. The 2p subshell is full. In 3p⁵, two orbitals have paired electrons and the third has a single unpaired electron, so Cl• is a free radical; the unpaired electron is in the 3p subshell.

book_ref.quote: In the 3p subshell, two orbitals have paired electrons whereas the third one contains a single unpaired electron.

blocks.text: 2.10 Electronic configuration and the formation of semiconductors

blocks.prompt: 64 What are semiconductors? Name two elements that act as semiconductors and two uses.
blocks.explanation: Semiconductors are materials that can conduct electricity under some conditions. Examples: silicon and germanium. They are used in electronic devices such as smartphones and laptops.

book_ref.quote: They are used in many electronic devices, including smartphones, laptops, and cars.

blocks.prompt: 65 Why does a pure silicon crystal not conduct electricity?
blocks.explanation: ₁₄Si = 2, 8, 4: it has 4 valence electrons. In the pure crystal each Si atom is bonded to four other Si atoms, so all valence electrons are used in bonds and there is no possibility of electronic conduction.

book_ref.quote: there is no possibility of electronic conduction through the Si crystal

blocks.prompt: 66 What is doping? Which impurities give P-type and which give N-type semiconductors?
blocks.explanation: Doping is adding impurity atoms to a pure semiconductor. Trivalent impurities (boron, aluminium) give P-type; pentavalent impurities (phosphorus, arsenic) give N-type.

book_ref.quote: P-type and N-type semiconductors are formed by

blocks.prompt: 67 Differentiate between P-type and N-type semiconductors.
blocks.explanation: P-type uses a trivalent impurity and holes; N-type a pentavalent impurity and extra electrons.

book_ref.quote: Some of the trivalent atoms take place of the Si atoms in the crystals.

rows: Doped with trivalent impurity (three valence electrons), e.g. B, Al
Doped with pentavalent impurity (five valence electrons), e.g. P, As
Si atoms near the impurity cannot make four bonds: holes are created
Four bonds form and the fifth electron is extra

blocks.prompt: 68 How does a P-type semiconductor conduct electricity?
blocks.explanation: Trivalent atoms (like Al) replace some Si atoms; Si cannot make four bonds due to the lack of electrons, so holes are created which act as positive charge carriers. Electrons from an external current source can then move through the semiconductor, and it acts as a conductor.

book_ref.quote: Electrons from an external current source can move through the semiconductor

blocks.prompt: 69 In N-type silicon doped with phosphorus, why does the fifth valence electron of phosphorus become free?
blocks.explanation: Phosphorus has five valence electrons. Four are used to make four bonds with neighbouring Si atoms; the fifth is an extra electron not needed for bonding, so it becomes free to move and acts as a negative charge carrier.

book_ref.quote: These impurity atoms contribute extra electrons to the crystal lattice
